title: Choose Wisely
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino argues that good teaching techniques can be undermined by poor choices of examples and analogies. She tells the story of a teacher who explains root hair cells by comparing them to Mr Nosey and uses cold calling, cues and summary well, yet weeks later students write about noses. The point is that where and how a technique is used matters, and a funny comparison can shift attention from the content to something irrelevant. She admits doing the same herself and gives three test questions: does it share relevant similarities, are its differences easy to explain, and does it detract from the focus. The conclusion is to choose wisely so the trick does not become the focus. It is Learning & Curriculum because it is about explanation and memory.
points: Sound moves like cold calling and cues can still fail if the example used distracts from the content.
Students remember the memorable hook, so irrelevant analogies replace the target knowledge in their answers.
Three checks help: relevant similarities, easily explained differences, and no distraction from the focus.
Examples and analogies deserve the same care as narrative tangents.
quotes: Cold Calling, thinking time, providing cues, summarising are all good things to do when teaching. But where and how we use them matters.

Before she explains where it is found and what it does, she notices the class looking bored, almost glassy-eyed. So, pointing to the picture of the root hair cell, she asks them: Which Mr Men character does this cell remind you of?

Miss K is pleased to see some of her students have remembered that root hair cells have a large surface area and that they absorb water. She is annoyed at the ones who have written about noses but thinks that as some students got the correct answer, the others don’t really have an excuse.

I have certainly done this in my own teaching before. I have given an example or made a funny comparison to something that shifts attention away from the actual content to something completely irrelevant.
I have previously written about the dangers of going off on tangents when narrating stories during teaching but we need to be just as careful with our examples and analogies.
We need to choose wisely when using examples and tricks and cues in teaching. Otherwise the things we say to make the content seem interesting become the focus, instead of the content itself.
